Structural graph theory.rationale: Favor global structural conjectures and the complexity of graph identity. Exact matching, flow and sparsity barriers lead the algorithmic remainder; close variants and specialized class restrictions follow.

selected.reason: Hadwiger’s conjecture proposes an exact relation between two basic graph parameters: the number of colors needed and the size of a complete graph obtainable by contraction. It extends the Four-Color Theorem and would turn exclusion of a complete minor into the sharp universal coloring bound. Its significance comes from this structural connection across all finite graphs, rather than from an algorithmic requirement in the question.
Tests whether the central equivalence problem for finite combinatorial structures can be recognized in deterministic polynomial time after the quasipolynomial barrier was broken.

Cryptography.rationale: Favor minimal assumptions for central cryptographic capabilities and information-theoretic limits. Keep secret sharing beside computational assumptions; place specialized efficiency improvements after broad primitive separations.

selected.reason: One-way functions are a basic foundation for computational pseudorandomness and cryptography. This question asks whether a worst-case separation between decision and verification already forces a function whose efficiently generated outputs resist inversion on average, without a separate cryptographic assumption.

This asks whether the minimal generic assumption supporting private-key cryptography also supports encryption to a receiver whose encryption key is public. It tests whether the apparent need for additional structure in public-key constructions reflects a true difference in existence or only the known reductions. The distinction controls the foundational assumptions needed for confidential communication without a pre-existing shared secret.

General indistinguishability obfuscation supports cryptographic capabilities well beyond ordinary encryption. Deriving it from one standard noisy-linear-equation assumption would connect that broad power to a much simpler foundation. The precise quantitative premise matters: an implication from stronger security or from secret-dependent hints does not determine the power of ordinary polynomial-hard LWE.

selected.topic: Unleveled fully homomorphic encryption from LWE alone
selected.reason: Determine whether ordinary LWE alone supports compact encrypted computation at arbitrary polynomial depth with one fixed key set.

selected.topic: Sub-square-root share-size exponents in perfect secret sharing
selected.reason: A worst-case storage benchmark for information-theoretic access control, separating the power of general secret sharing from linear schemes. The newly reported bound directly addresses its strict exponential threshold.

Differential privacy.rationale: Favor general private learnability and the computational limits of releasing rich statistical information. Sequential privacy costs remain important but follow these broader boundaries.

selected.topic: Private PAC sample complexity from VC and Littlestone dimensions
selected.reason: The theorem characterizing whether private learning is possible leaves an enormous quantitative gap. This question asks whether the extra data needed for privacy is controlled by ordinary statistical complexity and an exceptionally slowly growing function of sequential complexity. A positive answer would put a uniform bound on that privacy overhead across all finite concept classes.

selected.topic: Polynomial-time private release of all marginals
selected.reason: Marginals are basic summaries of relationships among attributes. The question asks whether the large information-theoretic usefulness of private high-dimensional data can be captured by a compact, efficiently evaluated object using polynomially many records. It isolates a statistical-versus-computational gap for a concrete query family while allowing outputs more flexible than synthetic datasets.
